newsitem.title: CHINA: HK court delays child immigrant deportation case.
newsitem.headline: HK court delays child immigrant deportation case.

text.p: A court on Monday postponed a landmark case on the deportation of illegal child immigrants which threatens to spark a fresh constitutional dilemma in Hong Kong, newly unified with China.

But another potential crisis could soon emerge with the territory's Beijing-installed Provisional Legislature likely to face a legal challenge for exceeding its powers, one of China's prominent political advisers said.

The two cases are testing the legal and constitutional arrangements which have been in place in Hong Kong since the former British colony became a Special Administrative Region (SAR) of China on July 1.

Hong Kong's High Court postponed making a decision on claims by young illegal immigrants from mainland China that a new law to deport them violates the SAR constitution by trampling on their right of abode.

Judge Brian Keith said he wanted to pick several cases which would cover all the legal questions to be decided. The hearing adjourned for a week after lawyers and the Justice Department failed to agree on test cases to be put forward.
Similar lawsuits are expected from hundreds of children. Some 100 "child illegals" have been granted government aid to finance their challenges.

The problem arose when the government passed a law to deport hundreds, and possibly thousands, of children who sneaked in to Hong Kong from China to avoid immigration formalities which take years to complete.
The children were smuggled into Hong Kong to join parents already here. Hong Kong wants them to go back to the mainland and apply for immigration papers through proper legal channels.
But if they have a Hong Kong parent with residency rights, then under the post-colonial constitution, the Basic Law, they themselves have the right of abode.
An estimated 66,000 children from divided families are waiting in China to join parents in Hong Kong. Formalities are often delayed by demands for bribes by Chinese officials.
Social activists and legal experts in Hong Kong have condemned the new law as unconstitutional because it rescinds retroactively rights conferred by the constitution.

Lau Siu-kai, a prominent member of the China-appointed Preparatory Committee which crafted the post-colonial power structures, said the interim legislature had exceeded its powers and might face a legal challenge.

When China decided to set up the Provisional Legislature to replace the existing Legislative Council, its scope was limited to passing the "minimum necessary" laws to ensure the smooth functioning of the post-colonial government until new elections are held.

Lau told reporters the legislature had exceeded its limits by freezing labour rights laws a week after China resumed sovereignty, launching debates on livelihood and economic issues, and setting up parliamentary panels.
Lau said none of these actions was urgently needed. "The trend is dangerous," he added.
Politicians from the pro-democracy camp have threatened to sue the legislature for exceeding its powers.
Last week a court crushed the first constitutional challenge to the legitimacy of the provisional legislature -- in which lawyers had argued there was a legal vacuum in Hong Kong.
